**Where characters are, and what they speak (decided 21 October 2026).** A shortage of characters now slows the game and makes service dearer; it no longer stops it, since couriers, caravans, ships, levies and policing do a kingdom's routine work, and only a voice or judgement needs a character. Where the shortage falls is shaped twice. Characters gather where the money is, at rich courts and on the trade roads. And they serve only where they can be understood: a character trades anywhere, since markets need no language, but carries a letter to a court or serves there only if he speaks its language or the lingua franca, and he learns a language only by living there ("Languages"). So a court with a rare tongue finds fewer servants and pays more for them: Pharaoh wrote to Arzawa in Hittite, not Akkadian (EA 31). Language is a character's capital, and years spent at a court make him worth more there. Learning has a price: a character may go to a court on his own and live there to learn, but he pays his own living and earns nothing meanwhile, a cost in gold and in what he could have earned. So the better ways in are paid ones: posted there as an envoy or resident by a king, the usual way in; trading in its market, which needs no language, so he earns while he learns; or, unluckily, held there as a captive or a detained envoy, who comes home with the language at least. No rule is needed: living costs and fees already set the price. Kings have the matching move: posting a new envoy abroad is also an investment in a future servant who speaks the language, much as Thutmose III had the sons of Levantine rulers raised at his court and sent home to rule (a precedent only, since the game has no heirs). Two things to measure, in items 11b, 12 and 18: how many seasons each court's letters wait for a carrier who can be understood where they are going, and whether fees rise until service pays again when working for oneself pays better ("Fees clear the market").

**Fees clear the market (decided 21 October 2026).** No rule sets the price of work. Characters are hired for jobs with a fee ("Jobs, not wages" in the main tab), and each kind of job has a going rate: when demand is greater than supply, employers outbid each other and fees rise; when supply is greater, fees fall. The able are always scarce ("Enough people, not enough good ones"), so their price rises furthest.

**Working for oneself (decided 21 October 2026).** A character's outside option is to serve no king. Characters already play for wealth ("Stakes, not dispositions"), so each compares what service pays with what he can earn on his own: dealing with other characters ("Characters deal with each other"), selling news ("Characters as sellers of news"), lending ("Lending to kings", "Lending to anyone"), forging on commission, mercenary work and escorting, interpreting at a posted price ("A go-between for hire"), ransom brokering, and outlawry ("Turning outlaw", "Pirates and bandits"). When fees are low, enterprise pays better and characters leave service; when kings pay well, they come back. Nobody is told to become a merchant: it pays or it does not. Two conditions. Enterprise must pay enough to be chosen but not so much that no king can hire, which the first guesses must leave room for and item 18 tunes. And script characters choose between service and enterprise by comparing expected income, or the feature does not count as built ("Every feature is every seat's"). A character working for himself can employ others too ("Anyone can hire anyone").

**No commander, no mandate.** An army needs a person to carry the king's intent. Near the king, he commands it directly; far away, an army without a commander has nobody to give a mandate to (decided 20 October 2026). It still follows plain orders, to the letter: it moves where it is told, holds where it is told, attacks where it is told, and supports as it is told, when the order reaches it, and a schedule of such orders runs as written. What it lacks is judgment: no intent to pursue, no standing orders, no adapting when things change. If the order no longer fits, because the city has fallen or an enemy stands in the way, it marches, bounces or holds as the order and the engine decide. Fighting needs no decision: an army that meets an enemy fights as the rules of combat say, commander or not. A commander is what turns orders into intent, so a shortage of commanders has a visible cost without any special rule.

**Standing orders belong to commanders** (decided 20 October 2026; built with command at a distance, build order item 13). Since the fix pass of 20 October, a standing order answers a rival's move in the season it is made, for every seat, defensively, once, on what the king can see. That is a reflex wired from the king to his troops wherever he is, which internal distance and commanders must change:

1. **It is part of a commander's mandate**, the king saying in advance "if this happens, do that". The commander with the army carries it out, or the king himself if he is there. An army with no commander present does not react ("No commander, no mandate").
2. **It comes into force only when it reaches the army.** A king in Babylon who writes one for a border army sends it there, and it holds from its arrival, like any order inside his realm, so contingencies must be planned early, and a king who moves his court to the front has faster reflexes there and slower ones everywhere else.
3. **It fires on what the army can see**, where its troops stand and one province around, not on everything the king sees.
4. **The commander's traits shape how it is carried out**, as for any mandate: loyalty sets how strictly he keeps to it, so a disloyal commander may look the other way; competence sets how well he reads the moment, so a poor one may answer a feint that a good one sees through.

Commanders become worth choosing well, since a good plan is only as good as the man carrying it out. Script kings give standing orders through their commanders too ("Every feature is every seat's").

**Hiring as a negotiation.** Today a king asks for candidates, up to three random free characters pitch from wherever they are, kings bid blind, and the highest bid at or above the asking price wins. Nobody travels, nobody haggles, and nobody learns there was a bidding war. Instead:

- **Characters travel to volunteer,** to courts that are hiring, where their sympathy lies, or away from danger, and the journey takes time like an envoy's.
- **They pitch in person and can play courts against each other:** "the king of Babylon offered me 30 shekels." It may be true or a lie.
- **Checking takes time, and the candidate may not wait.** A background check or a question to one's own envoy at Babylon takes seasons, and meanwhile the character may move on to another court. The king weighs verifying against losing the candidate. One round of negotiation a season; holding out costs the character time too.
- **Punishment has a price.** A king who catches a liar may execute him and take his purse and whatever he carried. But the execution spreads as a rumour, carried by whoever was at court, and characters grow wary of that court: the timid stay away, and the rest ask more to come. Harshness deters cheats and frightens honest talent alike; leniency attracts both. Executing someone whose claim turns out to be true is worse still. Gentler options exist: dismissing him, or exposing the lie to other courts, which damages his reputation instead of the king's.

**Characters have ongoing costs,** so purses do not grow into fortunes worth killing for:

- living costs each season, higher at rich courts;
- travel costs per journey;
- spending shaped by traits: the ambitious keep followers, the greedy hoard but are robbed or cheated more often, some send money home or pay old debts (the hidden fact "owes a debt to a copper trader" already exists);
- outlaws on the roads, and a bandit chief's band to feed.

A purse stays hidden, so a king never knows exactly what an execution would gain.

**Where characters keep their gold** (decided 19 October 2026; costs and lending added the same day). Gold is simulated as located amounts, and a character can take his where he wants. There are three ways to keep it, and choosing among them is the character's own decision. Each costs something and fails in its own way:

- **A purse on his person:** at hand wherever he goes, and earning nothing. Carried alone it costs nothing but is easily robbed on the road, which gives outlaws something worth hunting. An escort makes robbery harder and costs a fee for every journey, more the more he carries, so carrying with company is the dearest way to keep gold. It is seized when he is captured and taken if he is executed.
- **A hoard in one city he chooses,** kept with a temple or a merchant house, as Assyrian merchants kept their accounts at Kanesh, for a storage fee every season: safer than the road, but seized if that city's king turns on him, and lost if the city falls. It earns nothing, so it shrinks by the fee. Moving gold between purse and hoard takes him there.
- **Lent to a king, against a debt tablet:** the only way that earns. It costs nothing to keep, and its risk is the borrower: he may never repay, and if his kingdom falls the debt dies with it. See "Lending to kings" below.

**Lending to kings** (decided 19 October 2026). A character wants more gold, but he cannot put gold to work the way a king can: a king buys cities, raises troops and holds an army together through a lean season. So the character lends to a king, at an interest he sets himself. Lending is then the safest way he has to keep gold, and the only one that earns, where purse and hoard only cost.

- **What the engine knows.** The gold moves from the lender to the king's treasury, and travels like any gold. A debt tablet, sealed by both, records who owes whom and the sum to be repaid, interest included. Nothing forces repayment, and the score counts what each side holds, so the borrowed gold counts as the king's until he pays it back ("Debts are facts; repayment is a choice" in the main tab, as changed on 21 October 2026). The tablet is an object in a place like any other, and the lender keeps it.
- **What is only words.** The interest, the due date, collateral (a hostage, a city's yield sent each season, a post at court), what happens on default and any renegotiation are agreed at the audience or written on the tablet, and nothing enforces them. A king may refuse to pay and keep the gold. What he risks is what the world does about it: the lender's word, backed by the tablet anyone can read; the tablet sold to someone who can collect; and dearer credit, or none, the next time he needs it.
- **The lender's leverage** after a default is what he knows and where he can go: a rival court, an outlaw's life, the secrets he tells. Before that, a lender has a stake in his debtor's survival, which gives him reasons to warn him, spy for him or carry his letters faithfully.
- **Interest comes out of play.** The risk is the borrower: a strong king whose word holds borrows cheaply, a weak king at war pays steeply or finds no lender. No rule sets rates.
- **Kings and their debts.** For now a king dies only with his kingdom ("A kingdom falls with its capital" in the main tab), so a borrower can repay, default or fall, and when his kingdom falls its debts die with it. Because the debt is the kingdom's, not the king's, once rulers can die it passes to the heir with the rest of the old king's promises ("Succession"), who decides whether to honour it. Once "The capital is wherever the king is" is built, a king who leads from the front is easier for a lender to reach and riskier to lend to.
- **Model and script characters.** Model characters decide for themselves whether to lend, to whom and at what interest. Script characters roll it from their traits, such as greed and caution.
- **The period agrees.** Lending silver at interest was ordinary in Mesopotamia long before Amarna; Hammurabi's laws capped interest on silver at 20%, and set out how a deposit was made, before witnesses and with a written contract.

**The debt tablet is the claim** (decided 19 October 2026):

1. **Whoever holds the tablet holds the claim.** It is an object in a place, so it changes hands as objects do: taken from a captured or murdered lender, by whoever is with him when he dies, or from wherever he kept it, as when a city's lord seizes a hoard. Killing the lender settles nothing; getting the tablet does. A borrower who gets his own tablet has cancelled the debt, as a repaid loan's tablet was broken in the period. Gold paid to whoever brings the tablet repays it, and the tablet goes to the king, so a king may find a thief or a stranger at his door with his debt, and must decide whether to pay. A forged debt tablet falls under the existing forgery and examination rules, and works both ways: a forger can bring a false claim to a king, who may pay or pay to have the seal examined, and a king can show a forged "returned" tablet to claim a debt is settled. The engine knows the true seals, so only a genuine tablet is a true claim, and a forged copy cancels nothing.
2. **When a lender dies of his own accord,** the tablet stays where he kept it. On his person at a court, it passes to that court, so a king may come to hold a rival's debt, or his own, which cancels it. In his hoard, it stays with the temple or merchant house, where the city's lord may take it with the rest. On his person alone on the road, it goes missing. A missing tablet can never be collected, but the borrower learns that only when the news reaches him, so his own ledger shows the debt until then.
3. Settled (19 October 2026): escort fees, storage fees and how much an escort lowers the chance of robbery are not fixed in advance. The builder starts from a reasonable first guess, and balance tests tune them.

Where a man keeps his hoard says where his loyalty lies, and it gives that city's king leverage: a servant whose wealth sits in Hattusa thinks twice about betraying Hatti. It also gives outlaws a reason to watch for rich envoys on the road.

**Characters deal with each other** (decided 19 October 2026). Until now every market is a king buying from a character. Characters in the same place can also exchange messages and whatever they have on their person, which is little to build and gives model characters room to plan. Their talk follows the speaking rule (decided 21 October 2026): a message passes once they understand each other, which each season is a chance from the poorer of the two in their best shared language ("Speaking"). With no shared language they can still hand over this for that by gesture, which needs no talk ("No faceless channel"), but bargaining, news and promises wait for a go-between ("A go-between for hire") or for one of them to learn.

- **Same place only:** the same court, or the same province on the road. Nobody talks across the map (pillar 4).
- **Words are words, objects are facts.** Messages, offers and promises are free text and bind nobody. Gold, tablets and anything else carried move only through the engine.
- **Handed over in person, at once.** When both agree to the same exchange ("20 shekels for that tablet"), both sides change hands together. A promise to pay later is only words, and can be broken like any other.
- **No extra calls.** A character makes at most one approach a season, inside his own decision, and the other answers in his next one; script characters answer by formula from their traits, so every kind of character can deal.
- **Meetings can be seen.** Others in the same place may notice a meeting by chance, and what they saw becomes something they know and can sell ("What servants know"), so dealing in secret is never quite safe.

This opens markets among characters (debt tablets sold on, news bought, stolen goods fenced, a forger's commission, an outlaw recruiting), envoys of several courts waiting at one court comparing notes or selling each other out, and conspiracies, such as two envoys agreeing to send home the same false report.

**Lending to anyone (decided 21 October 2026).** The debt tablet works between any two parties: a character can lend to a character as he lends to a king, by the same rules ("Lending to kings", "The debt tablet is the claim"). Nothing tells anyone to lend. A loan happens when it pays both sides, and even before characters have ventures to fund, that happens in four ways:

- **Need.** A character who has hit the wall, unpaid, far from his hoard, with living costs due, a ransom to raise or an escort to pay, borrows at a steep rate rather than starve, turn outlaw or lose a captive. Desperation sets his price, as risk sets a king's.
- **Gathering.** A king needs sums larger than any one character holds. A character others trust can borrow from many at a modest rate and lend the whole to a king at a higher one, keeping the difference. He is a banker because it pays, not because the game names him one, and he carries the risk: if the king defaults, he still owes the people who lent to him, so one default can run down a chain of tablets. The Old Assyrian merchants of Kanesh pooled investors' gold for a venture in this spirit, some five centuries before Amarna.
- **Place.** Gold is located, and moving it takes travel and risk. A character whose hoard is in Babylon and who needs gold at Thebes can borrow at Thebes against it and repay later, which is worth paying for.
- **Ventures.** Once characters can put gold to work for themselves ("Working for oneself"), funding them becomes an alternative to lending to kings, and lenders choose between them by risk and return.

A script lender weighs a loan by formula: the expected return against the borrower's record, wealth and reputation. A script borrower borrows when his need, or his use for the gold, is worth more than the interest, so the gathering lender arises among script characters too whenever the difference pays ("Every feature is every seat's"). As for the kings, what a character owes or is owed counts for nothing in "The richest characters": the tablet is evidence and a claim, not an entry in the score. A loan pays the lender only once it is repaid, and a borrower who keeps the gold has it, and answers to the world for it.

**By word or by tablet.** A loan needs no tablet: two characters can agree it in words, and the gold moves like any gift. A word costs nothing and proves nothing. There is nothing to make, carry or lose, but if the borrower does not pay, the lender's accusation is his word against the borrower's. A tablet costs something, must be kept somewhere and can be stolen, but anyone can read it, so it is evidence, and a claim that can be sold ("Debts are facts; repayment is a choice" in the main tab). So small loans between people who trust each other tend to go by word, and large loans, or loans to strangers and kings, by tablet; nothing sets which. Hammurabi's laws asked for witnesses and a written contract for a deposit for the same reason.

**Time for script characters.** Model characters weigh the ending and the dangers of their own lives for themselves. Script characters would otherwise all reach the same expectation from the same formula, and no loan would pass between them, so each weighs time by a horizon of his own: how dangerous the life he leads is, and an impatience the engine derives from his traits, as a first guess tuned in item 18. An outlaw chief, a spy or a soldier can expect to die sooner, values gold now and borrows; a merchant with a hoard at a temple values gold later and lends. This is time preference, the root of interest, and needs no rule about the ending. It is not the same as appetite for risk ("Bold or careful, one goal"), though a bold man's dangerous life shortens his horizon too.

**Anyone can hire anyone (decided 21 October 2026).** Hiring is one contract whoever pays: a king, a city-state or a character, with the same jobs and fees, offers, loyalty and quitting ("Jobs, not wages" in the main tab). A character pays his people from his purse or hoard, wherever his gold is; one who does not pay what he promised gets the name of it, and his people leave him as they would leave a king. This is what lets enterprise grow: a dealer hires a guard for the road, a lender an agent to collect from a debtor, a captain the men of his band, a rich man a spy on the king who owes him. Hiring is for named people, the characters. Soldiers are not characters but men in a unit: a power levies them from its land, and a character gathers them into a band ("Bands are a character's soldiers"). What stays with powers is what comes from holding land: levies, garrisons and sealing for a kingdom.

**People of the land (decided 21 October 2026).** Each province's people are counted in three groups, one number each:

- **Settled:** the people on the land. They bring in the yield. Among them the men of fighting age are a number of their own, and every use of men draws on them: levies, police, builders whether paid or levied, porters, couriers and crews. Taking them hurts the harvest more than their share of the people, and how much follows the season: most at sowing and harvest, least in the slack months, which is when Egypt built, during the flood ("Seasons"). That is the only split by age or sex the game needs, since it is the one that changes decisions, and boys coming of age already carry a lost generation ("Births").
- **Under arms:** levied men away from their fields: soldiers in an army, porters, guards and couriers in caravans and the realm's courier service, and workers levied for building, the corvée (decided 21 October 2026). Each unit remembers the province it was drawn from, and its men go home there when it is disbanded.
- **Loose:** the landless, such as runaways, deserters, the displaced and the poor. They form bands, and loose men nobody has gathered are the province's banditry ("Pirates and bandits").

How the groups change:

- **Levying** moves settled people under arms, and the province's yield falls while they are away, so a long war costs harvests. Disbanding sends them home.
- **Battle counts its dead and its runaways.** A unit that loses a battle loses men: some die, which takes them from their home province and its men of fighting age for good, and some run, becoming loose men where the battle was lost. A dislodged unit loses fewer than a destroyed one, and the winner loses some too. Sieges and storming kill townspeople as well as soldiers.
- **Famine, plague and war** kill settled people or push them off the land.
- **Peace, good harvests, investment and policing** bring loose men back to the land, or suppress them.
- **Births** let a province grow back slowly towards what its land can carry, so a ravaged province recovers over years, not seasons. Boys coming of age restore the men of fighting age more slowly still, over about a generation, so a great war leaves a lost generation for the rest of most games.
- **Recruiting** a band, or hiring mercenaries, draws on the loose.
